topic: 3 signs your back pain is probably not serious

slides.headline: Back's gone. Should you panic?
slides.sub: Three signs it's the common, settles-on-its-own kind.

slides.title: First, the reassuring bit
slides.body: The vast majority of back pain, even the kind that stops you standing up straight, is not a sign of damage. It's painful, it's scary, and it usually settles within a few weeks.

slides.title: Sign 1: it came on with a movement
slides.body: Bent to pick something up, twisted in the garden, sneezed. A clear moment it started, with no other symptoms, is the classic pattern for a strain that will calm down.

slides.title: Sign 2: it changes with position
slides.body: Worse sitting, better walking. Or the other way round. Pain that shifts with how you move is mechanical, and mechanical pain responds well to movement and time.

slides.title: Sign 3: it stays in the back
slides.body: Pain that sits across the lower back, maybe into one buttock, without pins and needles or weakness in the legs, is very rarely something that needs a scan.

slides.title: The few things that do need a check
slides.body: Numbness around the groin, trouble controlling bladder or bowel, leg weakness that's getting worse, fever, or pain after a serious fall. These are uncommon, but don't wait on them.

slides.headline: Want a plan, not a scan?
slides.body: Our physios assess what's driving it, get you moving safely on day one and give you a short routine that speeds things up. Milton and Sunnybank.

caption:
Back's gone. Should you panic? Probably not. 🙂

Most back pain, even the kind that has you shuffling to the car, is not damage. Three signs it's the common kind: it started with a movement (lifting, twisting, sneezing), it changes with position, and it stays in the back and buttock without pins and needles or weakness in the legs. That pattern responds to movement, reassurance and time, and scans rarely change the plan.

A few things do need checking promptly: numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes, leg weakness that's getting worse, fever, or pain after a serious fall. Uncommon, but worth knowing.

topic: Stiff upper back from sitting

slides.headline: Upper back feels like a brick?
slides.sub: Three desk-side moves that loosen it in under two minutes.

slides.title: Why it stiffens up
slides.body: The mid back is built to rotate and extend. Sit still and slightly slumped for a few hours and it simply stops doing either. Stiffness, not damage.

slides.title: 1. Seated rotation
slides.body: Sit tall, cross your arms over your chest, turn to look behind you. Hold two breaths, swap sides. Five each way.

slides.title: 2. Chair extension
slides.body: Hands behind your head, lean back over the top of the chair backrest. Small range, no forcing. Ten slow reps.

slides.title: 3. Wall angels
slides.body: Back against a wall, arms in a goalpost shape, slide them up and down without the arms leaving the wall. Ten reps.

slides.title: What an adjustment adds
slides.body: Manual therapy can free up a stiff segment quickly, which makes the exercises above easier to do well. It works best alongside movement, not instead of it.

slides.headline: Still stiff after a week?
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess how your mid back, neck and shoulders move together and combine hands-on treatment with a short home routine.

caption:
Upper back feels like a brick by mid-afternoon? 🧱

The mid back is designed to rotate and extend. Sit slightly slumped for a few hours and it stops doing both, which is why it feels locked up. Stiffness, not damage.

Three quick fixes you can do at your desk: seated rotations, a gentle extension over the chair backrest, and wall angels. Two minutes, a couple of times a day. If it's still stiff after a week or so, hands-on treatment from a chiropractor can free up the stubborn segments so the exercises actually work.

topic: Clinical Pilates vs studio Pilates

slides.headline: Clinical Pilates or studio Pilates?

slides.title: Studio Pilates: group fitness

slides.title: Clinical Pilates: rehab first

slides.title: Can you do both?
slides.body: Yes, and heaps of people do. A common path is a block of clinical sessions to build confidence and control, then a gradual move into studio classes once things feel steady.

topic: Ankle sprain: why 'just rest it' is outdated

slides.headline: Rolled your ankle? Don't just rest it
slides.sub: Current guidelines favour early, gentle movement over weeks on the couch.

slides.title: Why the advice changed
slides.body: Older advice was to rest a sprained ankle until it felt normal. Current guidelines suggest protected, early movement usually helps ligaments recover and reduces stiffness and the chance of another sprain.

slides.title: The first few days
slides.body: Protect it, elevate it when you can and use compression if it helps the swelling. Walk as comfortably as you can, using a brace or crutches only if you genuinely need them.

slides.title: Days 3 to 14: get it moving
slides.body: Trace the alphabet with your toes, do gentle calf raises and practise standing on the injured leg near a bench. Mild discomfort is usually fine; sharp or worsening pain means ease off.

slides.title: Balance is the missing piece
slides.body: Many people stop once the swelling goes, but balance and strength often lag behind. Research suggests balance training can reduce the chance of another sprain, so keep it going for weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: You can't take four steps on it, there's tenderness right on the ankle bones, the foot looks misshapen, it's numb, or swelling isn't settling after a few days. Worth a prompt assessment.

slides.headline: Get a plan for your ankle
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios check the ankle, flag anything that needs imaging and map out your return to walking, running or sport.

Rolled your ankle? The old 'just rest it' advice is out of date.

The step most people skip is balance training. Research suggests it can lower the chance of rolling the same ankle again, so keep going after the swelling settles.

Get it checked promptly if you can't take four steps, the ankle bones are tender to touch, the foot looks misshapen or swelling isn't settling.

topic: The 'crack' sound during an adjustment explained

slides.headline: What's that crack during an adjustment?
slides.sub: Spoiler: it isn't bones grinding or anything popping back in.

slides.title: It's usually a gas bubble
slides.body: Joints are surrounded by fluid. When a joint is stretched quickly, pressure drops and a gas bubble forms in that fluid. That rapid change is what most researchers think makes the pop.

slides.title: It isn't bones moving back
slides.body: The sound doesn't mean a bone was out of place and has been put back. Joints don't slip out with everyday posture, and nothing is being realigned when you hear it.

slides.title: No crack doesn't mean no effect
slides.body: Some adjustments are quiet. Research suggests the sound isn't what makes an adjustment feel helpful, so chasing a louder pop isn't the goal. How you move afterwards matters more.

slides.title: Is cracking your own neck OK?
slides.body: An occasional self-crack is common and usually harmless. If you feel the urge constantly, that area is often stiff or tired, and regular movement and strength work tend to help more.

slides.title: Adjustments are one tool
slides.body: Our chiropractors combine hands-on treatment with exercise, advice and gradual loading. If you'd rather not be adjusted, just say so. There are gentler options, and you stay in control.

slides.headline: Curious, but a bit nervous?
slides.body: Our chiropractors at Hybrid Physiotherapy explain every step before they start, and you can ask questions at any point. Book online via the link in bio.

topic: Achilles tendon pain in runners

slides.headline: Achilles grumbling on your runs?
slides.sub: Tendons love load, just not sudden spikes of it.

slides.title: Why tendons get cranky
slides.body: Achilles pain in runners often follows a change: more kilometres, extra hills, speed work or new shoes. The tendon hasn't had time to adapt to the new load, so it lets you know.

slides.title: Rest alone rarely sorts it
slides.body: Tendons often calm down during rest, then flare again when you return. What usually helps is loading them progressively with strength work so they can handle running again.

slides.title: Start with calf raises
slides.body: Slow calf raises off a step, both legs and then single leg, are a common starting point. Some discomfort during exercise is often okay if it settles by the next morning.

slides.title: Use the morning check
slides.body: Stiffness first thing is a handy guide. If it's worse the morning after a run, scale back a bit. If it's the same or better, you can usually keep building gradually.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A sudden pop, or a feeling like you were kicked in the back of the leg, trouble walking or rising onto your toes, or major swelling. These need a prompt assessment.

slides.headline: Keep running while it settles
slides.body: Our Sunnybank and Milton physios assess your tendon and training, then build a strength and running plan that suits your week.

caption:
Achilles sore after your runs? Resting it probably won't be enough on its own.

Achilles pain in runners often follows a change in load: more kilometres, hills, speed work or new shoes. Tendons often calm down with rest, then flare again when you go back, because they haven't been built up to cope.

What usually helps is progressive loading. Slow calf raises off a step are a common place to start, and your morning stiffness is a useful guide to whether you're doing too much. Many runners can keep running at a reduced level while this happens.

A sudden pop or trouble rising onto your toes needs a prompt check.

topic: Shin splints: it's a load problem

slides.headline: Shin splints are a load problem
slides.sub: Why your shins complain and how to build them back up.

slides.title: What's usually going on
slides.body: Shin splints, or medial tibial stress syndrome, is pain along the inner edge of the shin. It often shows up when running load rises faster than bone and muscle can adapt.

slides.title: Common triggers
slides.body: A jump in weekly kilometres, returning after a break, more hard surfaces or extra sessions squeezed in before an event. Shoes often matter less than people think; the training pattern usually matters more.

slides.title: Adjust, don't necessarily stop
slides.body: Cutting back volume or intensity is often enough. Cycling, swimming or walking can keep fitness ticking over while the shins settle. Aim for runs that feel no worse the next day.

slides.title: Build capacity
slides.body: Calf raises, single-leg balance and hip strength work help your legs share the load. When you return, add distance gradually and avoid ramping up speed and volume at the same time.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain in one small spot on the bone, pain at rest or at night, or pain that makes you limp. These can point to a bone stress injury, so get assessed before running again.

slides.headline: Get back to running with a plan
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios look at your training, strength and running, then build a return plan you can actually follow.

caption:
Sore shins every time you up your kilometres? That's a clue.

Shin splints usually show up when running load rises faster than your bones and muscles can adapt: a jump in distance, a return after a break or a rush of extra sessions before an event.

The good news is you often don't have to stop completely. Trim volume or intensity, cross-train with cycling or swimming, and build calf and hip strength. Then add distance gradually, and don't lift speed and volume at the same time.

Pain in one small spot on the bone, pain at night or a limp needs checking before you run again.

slides.title: Remedial massage: a specific goal
slides.body: It starts with questions and a quick assessment. The therapist targets areas linked to your niggle, like a stiff neck from desk work or tight calves from running, using a range of techniques.

slides.title: It doesn't have to hurt
slides.body: Remedial can be firmer, but more pressure isn't always more helpful. Good remedial work stays at a level you can breathe through. Tell your therapist if it's too much at any point.

slides.body: Massage complements active rehab rather than replacing it. Many people feel looser after a session, and pairing it with simple stretches or strength work helps that feeling last longer.

topic: Heel pain with the first steps in the morning (plantar heel pain)

slides.headline: Those first steps out of bed hurt?
slides.sub: Morning heel pain is common, and it usually settles with the right load.

slides.title: What's often behind it
slides.body: Plantar heel pain involves the thick tissue under the foot where it attaches to the heel. That first-step pain after rest is a classic pattern, and it often eases once you get moving.

slides.title: Common contributors
slides.body: More time on your feet, a jump in walking or running, a change in footwear or stiff calves. It's common in runners and in people who stand for long shifts at work.

slides.title: Things to try today
slides.body: Supportive shoes around the house, a gentle calf and foot stretch before your first steps, and rolling your arch over a bottle. Ease back a little on activities that make it flare.

slides.title: Strength is the long game
slides.body: Slow heel raises with your toes on a rolled towel are a common starting exercise. Build them gradually over weeks. Research suggests strength work plus load changes helps most people improve.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain after a fall or a jump, noticeable swelling, numbness or tingling in the foot, heel pain at night, or pain in both heels along with other joint pain. Worth a proper assessment.

slides.body: Our Milton and Sunnybank physios check your foot, calf and loading, then set up an exercise program and footwear tips to help.

topic: Runner's knee: pain around the kneecap

slides.headline: Knee aching after runs or stairs?
slides.sub: Pain around the kneecap is common in runners, and very manageable.

slides.title: Meet runner's knee
slides.body: Patellofemoral pain is an ache around or behind the kneecap. It often flares with stairs, squats, hills or sitting for a long time with bent knees, like at the movies.

slides.title: It's usually a load issue
slides.body: It usually shows up when running or training increases faster than the knee can adapt. Scans often look normal, and it doesn't mean your knee is wearing out.

slides.title: Tweak your training
slides.body: Drop the hills and speed work for a bit, shorten your runs and slightly increase your step rate. Keep pain while running mild, and make sure it settles within a day.

slides.title: Strengthen hips and thighs
slides.body: Research suggests hip and thigh strengthening is one of the most helpful approaches. Try wall sits, step-ups and side-lying leg raises, building up gradually over several weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Swelling after a twist, a knee that locks or gives way, trouble fully bending or straightening it, or pain that keeps you up at night. These deserve a proper look.

slides.headline: Keep your knees in the game
slides.body: Our Sunnybank and Milton physios assess your knee, strength and running, then build a plan to get you back on track.

Pain around the kneecap is one of the most common running niggles. It usually appears when training ramps up faster than the knee can adapt, and it doesn't mean your knee is wearing out.

A few changes often help: ease off hills and speed work, shorten runs for a while, and lift your step rate slightly. Add hip and thigh strength work like wall sits and step-ups, and build gradually.

topic: ITB pain on the outside of the knee in runners

slides.headline: Outside-of-knee pain on longer runs?
slides.sub: ITB pain often kicks in at the same point each run. Here's why.

slides.title: What it usually is
slides.body: Iliotibial band pain is felt on the outside of the knee. It often starts a set distance into a run and can get sharp enough to stop you, then eases with rest.

slides.title: Why rolling isn't the answer
slides.body: The ITB is very strong connective tissue, so you can't really stretch or roll it longer. Rolling may feel good short term, but load changes and strength work usually matter more.

slides.title: Common triggers
slides.body: A quick jump in distance, lots of downhill running, running the same direction on a cambered road or track, or bunching hard sessions together. Look back at your last month of training.

slides.title: What to try
slides.body: Cut back distance for a while, skip downhills and stick to flat surfaces. Add hip strength work like side planks and single-leg squats, then build distance gradually once runs feel comfortable.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Swelling in the knee, locking or giving way, pain after a twist or fall, or pain that's there even when you're resting. These suggest something else may be going on.

slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your hips, knees and running pattern, then build a plan that fits your training.

topic: Rotator cuff pain: common myths

slides.headline: Rotator cuff pain: 4 myths to drop
slides.sub: What current guidelines actually say about sore shoulders.

slides.title: Myth: the scan tells all
slides.body: Plenty of people without shoulder pain have rotator cuff changes on scans, and they become more common as we age. A scan finding doesn't always explain your pain or decide your plan.

slides.title: Myth: rest it until it's gone
slides.body: Complete rest often leaves the shoulder stiffer and weaker. Keeping it moving within a comfortable range, and gradually loading it, usually helps more than keeping it still.

slides.title: Myth: rehab must be painless
slides.body: Some discomfort during rehab exercises is often okay. A common guide is pain that stays mild and settles within a day. Your physio can help you find the right level for you.

slides.title: Myth: avoid overhead forever
slides.body: Avoiding overhead movement for good can make it harder to return. Most people can gradually work back to reaching, lifting and overhead sport with a graded plan, starting lower and building up.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Sudden weakness after a fall or heavy lift, being unable to lift your arm, severe night pain, a misshapen shoulder, or pins and needles down the arm. Get these looked at promptly.

slides.headline: Get your shoulder moving again
slides.body: Our Milton and Sunnybank physios assess your shoulder and build a strength program that fits your work, gym or sport.

Sore shoulder and a scan that says 'rotator cuff'? Time to bust a few myths.

Some discomfort during rehab is usually okay if it settles within a day. And most people can gradually get back to overhead work and sport.

Current guidelines put exercise and gradual loading at the centre of rotator cuff care.

topic: Clinical Pilates for lower back pain: what the research suggests

slides.headline: Can Pilates help lower back pain?
slides.sub: What the research suggests, minus the hype.

slides.title: What the research suggests
slides.body: Current guidelines recommend exercise as a first-line approach for persistent lower back pain. Research suggests Pilates-based exercise can help reduce pain and improve function, much like other well-designed exercise.

slides.title: No single type wins
slides.body: Studies generally don't show one exercise style clearly ahead of the others. The type you enjoy and keep doing, progressed sensibly, often matters more than the name on the class.

slides.title: It's not about a weak core
slides.body: Back pain isn't simply caused by a weak core. Pilates can help by building strength, confidence and comfortable movement, so everyday tasks feel less threatening to your back.

slides.title: Why clinical matters here
slides.body: Clinical Pilates starts with an assessment, and exercises are adapted to your symptoms and goals. That can make it easier to start if you're worried about flaring things up.

slides.title: Get a medical check first if
slides.body: Back pain comes with numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes, leg weakness that's getting worse, fever or unexplained weight loss. These need checking before any exercise program.

topic: Frozen shoulder: what to expect and how long it lasts

slides.headline: Frozen shoulder: what to expect
slides.sub: It's slow and frustrating, but most people do get their movement back.

slides.title: What it is
slides.body: Frozen shoulder is when the capsule around the shoulder joint becomes inflamed and tight. Movement gets painful and very limited in several directions. It's most common between about 40 and 60.

slides.title: Stage 1: the painful phase
slides.body: Pain builds, often worse at night, and movement starts to tighten. This phase can last several months. Gentle movement within comfort, heat, pillow support and pacing can help you cope.

slides.title: Stage 2: the stiff phase
slides.body: Pain often eases, but the shoulder stays tight. Reaching overhead or behind your back is hard. Regular gentle stretching and strength work help you keep function while it runs its course.

slides.title: Stage 3: the thaw
slides.body: Movement gradually returns. The whole process often takes many months, sometimes a year or two. Most people get back most of their movement, even if progress feels slow.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Shoulder pain after a fall, sudden loss of strength, fever, pain that's quickly getting worse, or arm pain with chest pain or breathlessness. That last one needs urgent medical care.

slides.headline: Stuck in the stiff stage?
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your shoulder, explain what stage it seems to be in and guide exercises that keep you moving.

caption:
Frozen shoulder is one of the slowest shoulder problems to settle. Here's what to expect.

It usually moves through three stages. First, a painful phase where movement starts to tighten and nights can be rough. Then a stiff phase, where pain eases but reaching overhead or behind your back is hard. Finally, a thaw, where movement gradually returns.

The whole process often takes many months and sometimes a year or two, but most people get back most of their movement. Gentle, regular exercise helps you keep function along the way.

topic: Tennis elbow: grip, load and patience

slides.headline: Tennis elbow? You don't need to play
slides.sub: Grip, load and patience: how outer elbow pain usually settles.

slides.title: What it usually is
slides.body: Lateral elbow pain comes from the tendons that attach on the outside of the elbow. It's common in people who grip a lot: mouse users, tradies, gym-goers and, yes, tennis players.

slides.title: Grip is the giveaway
slides.body: Pain gripping a kettle, opening jars or shaking hands is typical. Use a lighter grip where you can, lift with your palm facing up, and take regular micro-breaks from the mouse.

slides.title: Load it, don't baby it
slides.body: Tendons respond to gradual loading. Slow wrist exercises with a light dumbbell or band are a common starting point. Mild discomfort that settles by the next day is usually okay.

slides.title: Patience is part of the plan
slides.body: Tennis elbow is often slow to settle and can take months. Research suggests steady, progressive exercise helps most people improve over time, so stick with it even when progress feels slow.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain after a fall or a big lift, swelling or a clunk in the joint, numbness or tingling into the hand, or weakness when gripping. These are worth a proper assessment.

slides.headline: Get a grip on elbow pain
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios check your elbow, neck and workload, then build a loading program and practical desk tips.

caption:
You don't have to play tennis to get tennis elbow. A mouse, a tool or the gym is a far more common trigger.

Outer elbow pain comes from the tendons on the outside of the elbow, and gripping is usually what sets it off. Small changes help: a lighter grip, lifting with your palm up and micro-breaks at the desk.

Tendons respond to gradual loading, so slow wrist exercises are a common starting point. It can take months to settle, and steady, progressive work usually wins out.

Numbness into the hand or pain after a fall is worth checking.

topic: Sore after a massage: normal or not?

slides.headline: Sore the day after a massage?
slides.sub: Usually normal. Here's what's expected and what isn't.

slides.title: Some soreness is common
slides.body: Feeling a bit tender or achy for a day or two after remedial massage, especially after deeper work, is common. It often feels like mild post-gym soreness and eases on its own.

slides.title: What helps it settle
slides.body: Keep moving gently with a walk, easy stretches or light activity. A warm shower can feel nice. Most people find the soreness fades faster with movement than with staying still.

slides.title: What isn't normal
slides.body: Bruising you didn't expect, sharp pain, pins and needles, or soreness that's getting worse after two or three days. Let your therapist know, and see your GP if symptoms seem unusual.

slides.title: Pressure should be negotiable
slides.body: Firm isn't automatically more effective. Tell your therapist if the pressure feels too strong during the session. You can ask for lighter work and still get a useful remedial massage.

slides.title: Keep expectations realistic
slides.body: Massage can help you feel looser and move more comfortably for a while. It complements, rather than replaces, exercise and active rehab for a niggle that keeps coming back.

slides.headline: Questions before your session?
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists at Hybrid Physiotherapy are happy to talk through pressure and aftercare. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:

What isn't normal: unexpected bruising, sharp pain, pins and needles or soreness that gets worse after a couple of days. Let your therapist know, and see your GP if anything seems off.

Remember, you can always ask for lighter pressure. Massage works alongside exercise rather than replacing it.

topic: Knee osteoarthritis: why exercise beats another scan

slides.headline: Knee arthritis: why exercise comes first
slides.sub: Current guidelines put exercise and education ahead of repeat imaging.

slides.title: Scans rarely change the plan
slides.body: X-ray changes and pain often don't match well. Plenty of people with arthritis on imaging have little pain, and the reverse. Another scan usually won't change what helps day to day.

slides.title: Exercise is first-line
slides.body: Current guidelines recommend exercise and education as the first-line approach for knee osteoarthritis. Strength work and regular activity can help reduce pain and improve how well you get around.

slides.title: Moving is good for joints
slides.body: Joints are designed to be loaded. Research suggests appropriate activity is safe for knees with arthritis, and cartilage responds well to movement. Resting too much often makes stiffness worse.

slides.title: A simple place to start
slides.body: Sit-to-stands from a chair, step-ups on the bottom stair and regular walking are a good starting point. Some discomfort is usually okay if it settles within a day.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A hot, very swollen knee, fever, a knee that suddenly locks or gives way, or pain after a fall or twist. These need a prompt assessment rather than a home program.

slides.headline: Want a plan for your knees?
slides.body: Our Sunnybank and Milton physios assess your knees and build a strength program that fits your life and goals.

caption:
Knee arthritis? Another scan probably won't change much. Exercise often will.

topic: Sciatica vs ordinary back pain

slides.headline: Sciatica or ordinary back pain?
slides.sub: Where the pain travels gives useful clues. Here's how they usually differ.

slides.title: Ordinary back pain
slides.body: It usually sits across the lower back and maybe into the buttock. It often changes with position and movement, and most episodes settle over days to weeks when you stay active.

slides.title: What sciatica usually feels like
slides.body: Pain that travels down the leg, often below the knee, sometimes with pins and needles or numbness. The leg can hurt more than the back. It comes from an irritated nerve root.

slides.title: Both usually improve
slides.body: Sciatica can be more intense and take longer, often weeks to a few months. Still, most people improve with time, movement and conservative care. Staying gently active helps in both cases.

slides.title: What helps in the meantime
slides.body: Short walks, changing position often and gentle movements you can tolerate. Avoid long stretches of bed rest. Your physio can suggest positions and exercises that ease leg symptoms.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Numbness around the groin, changes in bladder or bowel control, leg weakness that's getting worse, or symptoms in both legs. These need urgent medical attention, so seek help straight away.

slides.headline: Not sure which you've got?
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your back and legs, explain what's going on and set up a plan to keep you moving.

caption:
Pain in your back, or pain running down your leg? The difference matters.

Ordinary back pain usually stays in the lower back and buttock and changes with position. Sciatica usually travels down the leg, often past the knee, sometimes with pins and needles or numbness, and the leg can hurt more than the back.

Both usually improve. Sciatica can take longer, but most people get better with time, movement and conservative care. Short walks and regular position changes tend to help more than bed rest.

Numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes or worsening leg weakness needs urgent medical attention.

topic: Tech neck: is it real?

slides.headline: Tech neck: real or overhyped?
slides.sub: What looking at your phone does, and doesn't, do to your neck.

slides.title: The honest answer
slides.body: Research hasn't shown that phone posture on its own causes neck pain. But long stretches in any one position can leave your neck stiff, tired and achy by the end of the day.

slides.title: Posture isn't the villain
slides.body: There's no single perfect posture. The problem is usually staying still for too long. Your next position is often the most helpful one, so change it up regularly through the day.

slides.title: Try the 30-minute reset
slides.body: Every half hour, roll your shoulders, turn your head side to side and look up at the ceiling. Hold your phone a little higher and set your screen at eye level.

slides.title: Build a stronger neck
slides.body: Simple exercises like chin tucks and shoulder blade squeezes, plus general strength work, help your neck tolerate long days. Regular movement usually helps more than holding a rigid posture.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Neck pain with pins and needles or weakness in the arms, dizziness, severe headaches, or pain after a fall or car accident. These need a proper assessment first.

caption:
Is 'tech neck' real? Sort of, but not in the scary way you've heard.

Research hasn't shown that looking at your phone on its own causes neck pain. What does tend to leave necks stiff and achy is staying in any one position for too long. There's no perfect posture, and your next position is often the most helpful one.

Try a quick reset every 30 minutes: shoulder rolls, head turns and a look up at the ceiling. Add simple neck and upper back strength work to help you handle long days.
